title: Accounting is the language of business
subtitle: Why every financial decision needs accounting
openingQuestion: You want to know whether a company is making money or losing it - what do you read?
explanation: Accounting is the shared set of conventions for describing a business in numbers, so that investors elsewhere, banks and management all read the same picture. Worth remembering from the start: this is a language with its own rules, and many of those rules don't match ordinary intuition - revenue isn't cash received, an expense isn't cash paid, and profit isn't cash left over.

realWorldExample.description: Vingroup publishes consolidated quarterly financial statements under IFRS - thousands of investors, banks and tax authorities read the same set of numbers to reach different decisions, proof that accounting is a shared language.

quiz.question: What are accounting standards (VAS, IFRS, US GAAP) for?
options: So the tax authority can calculate the exact corporate tax due
So financial statements from different places can be compared
So accountants have legal grounds to protect themselves when they err
So accounting software is standardised worldwide
quiz.explanation: Accounting standards are the shared rulebook that lets investors, banks and other stakeholders read statements from different companies and countries the same way.

quiz.question: Who are the main people who need to read and understand financial statements?
options: Only the tax authority, since this is a mandatory filing
Only management and the chief accountant inside the company
Investors, banks, tax authorities, employees
Only shareholders holding over 5% of the company
quiz.explanation: Accounting provides a shared language for everyone who makes decisions related to the company.

quiz.question: What is the difference between an accountant and a bookkeeper?
options: There is no difference at all - the two titles are just two names for the same job
A bookkeeper always has higher qualifications and credentials than an accountant
Accountants may only work in banking, never in manufacturing businesses
A bookkeeper records transactions; an accountant classifies, summarises and analyses to produce financial statements
quiz.explanation: Bookkeeping (detailed recording) is one part of accounting (the fuller discipline). Accountants do more: classifying, summarising, analysing to support decisions grounded in data.

quiz.question: What is double-entry bookkeeping for?
options: So every transaction is recorded from two sides, self-checking for balance
So two accountants record it separately and cross-check each other
So management accounting stays separate from financial accounting books
So two copies of the books exist in case one is lost
quiz.explanation: Double entry reduces errors because every transaction must balance: debit side = credit side. If it doesn't balance, something is wrong.

quiz.question: What are the three main financial statements?
options: Balance sheet, general ledger, and the payroll sheet
Income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement
Income statement, balance sheet, and the annual tax return
Income statement, cash flow statement, and the notes
quiz.explanation: The three statements: the income statement answers "profit or loss?", the balance sheet answers "what do we have and owe?", and the cash flow statement answers "how much real cash moved?"

quiz.question: Why must accounting comply with laws and standards?
options: So the company gets a reduction in corporate income tax
So accountants cannot be criminally prosecuted for errors
To ensure reliability and reduce fraud
So accounting software runs to the required template
quiz.explanation: Mandatory accounting standards help prevent fraud and ensure stakeholders can trust the data they read.

quiz.question: What does "earnings quality" mean in accounting?
options: Simply how high or low the profit figure on the income statement is
The number of times an accountant re-checks the profit figure before publishing it
The colours and formatting of the financial statements when printed
How much of the reported profit comes from real cash flow versus "paper profit"
quiz.explanation: A company can report high profit, but if it comes from revenue not yet collected in cash, earnings quality is poor. Profit backed by cash actually received has higher quality.

keyTakeaways: Accounting is the language of business - everyone should be able to read it
Financial statements are the output of the accounting system
You don't need to be an accountant to understand the basic numbers

practicePrompt.question: Your boss - who has no finance background - asks: 'Why does a marketer like me need to learn to read financial statements?' Which answer best matches the spirit of this lesson?
options: Because accounting is the shared language of business - understanding financial statements helps every role, not just accountants, make better decisions grounded in the company's actual situation
It isn't necessary, since reading financial statements is solely the job of the accounting and internal audit department
It's only necessary if marketing wants to move into a professional accounting career in the future
Only the CEO and CFO genuinely need to understand a company's financial statements
practicePrompt.explanation: Accounting is the language of business: everyone who makes decisions related to the company - not just accountants - needs to be able to read basic financial statements to correctly judge the real situation.

summary.keyIdea: Accounting is the language of business - everyone should be able to read it
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Try reading a financial statement
application.message: Open the financial statements of any listed company (on its investor relations page or a stock app) and try to name the three main statements you see, even before you understand the detail inside.
application.secondary: The goal here is just to recognise the shapes, not yet to understand them deeply.

sections.text: You can read a menu in Vietnamese because you know the Vietnamese alphabet. In the same way, you can only read the financial health of Vingroup, Vinamilk or FPT if you know the 'letters' of accounting - the shared language every business in the world uses to tell its own money story.

Every day, a business generates hundreds or thousands of transactions: sales, salary payments, raw material purchases, bank loans, payments to suppliers. Accounting is the system tasked with recording, classifying and summarising all of those transactions into structured reports - mainly three statements: the Balance Sheet, the Income Statement and the Cash Flow Statement.

Without accounting, a company with revenue of 50,000 billion dong like Vinamilk could not know precisely whether it is profitable or losing money, how much it owes, or what assets it truly holds. Accounting turns millions of separate transactions into a handful of summary numbers everyone can read and understand.

A language needs shared grammar so speaker and listener understand each other the same way. Accounting is the same - it has standards (VAS in Vietnam, IFRS in many countries, US GAAP in the US) that specify precisely when an item is recognised as revenue, an asset or an expense. Thanks to this shared standard, an investor in Hanoi can read the financial statements of a company in New York and understand the substance correctly, even without knowing anything about that company's actual operations.

items: Investors: read financial statements to decide whether to buy shares
Banks: read them to decide whether to lend, and at what interest rate
Tax authorities: read them to calculate corporate income tax owed
Management: read them to make operating, investment and cost-cutting decisions
Suppliers: read them to decide whether to extend trade credit

concepts.def: The system for recording, classifying and summarising an organisation's economic transactions.
The set of three summary reports: the balance sheet, the income statement, and the cash flow statement.
The shared rulebook for how financial items are recognised and presented.
Investors, banks, suppliers, tax authorities - everyone who needs to read financial statements.

sections.label: Don't be afraid of the numbers
sections.text: You don't need to become a professional accountant to read basic financial statements, just as you don't need to be a novelist to read a novel. This track will teach you to correctly read the numbers that matter most: revenue, expenses, profit, assets, liabilities and equity.

lines: Accounting isn't a subject only for finance people - it's a language everyone should be able to read.
The next 20 lessons will teach you that language letter by letter, starting with revenue and expenses.
